items.summary: Research data and software supporting the derivation and literature reconstruction of relative-sensitivity expressions in inverse multiple linear regression luminescence thermometry. Includes executable Excel calculations for 22 model-temperature cases from seven papers, literature classification and equation-lineage evidence, numerical reconstruction code, analytical figure data, editable figure sources, and preserved Lean 4 and AXLE verification records. Effective sensitivities are conditional on the stated reference noise model and recovered local gain. Unresolved reconstruction discrepancies and the limited scope of formal verification are documented.
items.title: Data and software for "A reciprocal-derivative error inflates relative sensitivity in multivariate luminescence thermometry"

items.summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. This version supersedes the earlier R-only archive by adding the Python utilities, complete operational documentation, software-environment records, random seeds, integrity checks, and portable figure-generation scripts.

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
items.title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

items.summary: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory Architecture manuscript. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling
items.title: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory

items.summary: # FaultNet This archive contains the trained models, example earthquake catalog, and Jupyter notebook used to apply **FaultNet**, a deep-learning framework for reconstructing three-dimensional fault structures from earthquake hypocenters. FaultNet uses two PointNet++-based models followed by agglomerative clustering and fault surface reconstruction by radial basis function. The first model, denoising model, identifies fault-related earthquakes and removes background seismicity. The second model, feature learning model, maps the remaining earthquakes into an embedding space in which earthquakes associated with the same fault have similar representations. Pairwise similarities estimated from overlapping spatial windows are combined into a global distance matrix and used for clustering. The resulting earthquake clusters can then be reconstructed as continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. ## Files and directories - `apply_FaultNet.ipynb`     Main notebook demonstrating the complete FaultNet inference workflow, including:   1. loading the trained models;   2. loading and visualizing an earthquake catalog;   3. selecting a sliding-window size;   4. identifying fault-related earthquakes;   5. learning feature embedding and agglomerative clustering;   6. reconstructing fault surfaces using RBF interpolation; and   7. evaluating and visualizing the reconstructed surfaces. - `example_catalog.npy`   Example earthquake catalog used in the notebook. The array has shape `(N, 5)`, with columns:   `x, y, z, horizontal_location_error, vertical_location_error`.   Spatial coordinates and location uncertainties should use consistent distance units (km in the provided example).   Users can replace it with another earthquake catalog following the same format. Coordinates and uncertainties should be expressed in a consistent Cartesian coordinate system and distance unit. - `example_prediction.npy`     Example FaultNet clustering output corresponding to `example_catalog.npy`. It contains one integer label per earthquake. A label of `-1` denotes background seismicity or clusters excluded by the minimum-size criterion (50 events); non-negative integers identify reconstructed fault clusters. - `model_I_denoising/`     Trained denoising model for distinguishing fault-related earthquakes from background seismicity. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `model_II_feature_learning/`     Trained feature learning model for generating 8-dimensional embedding representations of fault-related earthquakes. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `Pointnet_Pointnet2_pytorchmaster/`     PointNet++ implementation and supporting source code used by the FaultNet models. This directory is based on a PyTorch implementation of PointNet/PointNet++ and retains its associated license information. - `requirements.txt`     Python packages required by the main FaultNet notebook. ## Installation Python 3 is required. To install the main dependencies, run: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` The supplied notebook loads the trained neural networks on the CPU by default. PyTorch can be configured separately for CUDA-enabled GPU execution if desired.   ## Citation If you use FaultNet or the materials in this archive, please cite the associated FaultNet publication and this Zenodo record. .. 10.5281/zenodo.22837108 ## Acknowledgments This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (Award No. DE-SC0026319). ## License Please refer to the license information distributed with the relevant source-code components. Before public release, add the license selected for the FaultNet-specific code and trained models to the top-level archive.

items.summary: The article “The Image of Istanbul in the Russian Émigré, Soviet, and Modern Russian-Language Literature” explores various facets of the city’s image through the lens of the short stories and essays of the first wave of Russian émigrés’ literature, Soviet literary work of the 1920s-1930s, and contemporary Russian-language Azerbaijani prose. Literary works by Nadezhda Teffi Istanbul and the Sun (1921) and Gaito Gazdanov A Weak Heart (1927) explored in the article, focus on the émigré experience representing two most common ways of depicting Istanbul among the Russian émigré writers. Teffi neither succumbs to Orientalist fantasy nor reduces the city to a refugee misery, she supports both notions and considers Istanbul to be the city of exiles’ humiliation and artistic transcendence, whereas Gazdanov interprets the first center of Russian emigration more clearly and tragically, depicting it as a symbol of life without any moral support. Soviet literature portrays Istanbul in an entirely different manner. During the 1920s-1930s, the description of the East was ideologically justified as it implicitly prepared the ground for developing the internationalist theme of “the friendship of peoples”. Thus, Soviet writers focused mainly on the political, social, and cultural changes which occurred in Turkey during the 1920s, highlighting the country’s transformation from a historical enemy to potential ally. Sweet Salt of the Bosphorus (2008) by a contemporary Azerbaijani author Elchin Safarli who takes into account the artistic experience of Russian émigrés, creates a transcultural space that exhibits the following features of transliterary writing: the author’s specific bilingual linguistic consciousness, the reconstruction of an Azerbaijani worldview through the Russian language, an interlinguistic textual field, the foregrounding of the cultural integration of Russians in the East and an objective reconstruction by the writer, who belongs to the Eastern cultural code, of a “Russian” perspective on the world.
items.title: Image of Istanbul in the Russian émigré, Soviet, and modern Russian-language literature

items.summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.
items.title: Stability Architectures: A Finite Classification of Provable Cases

items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
items.title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

items.summary: Abstract Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: How Artificial Intelligence Industrializes the Colonial Erasure of Global Majority Knowledge Systems Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz Decolonial Social Scientist | Developer, Justice AI GPT | Architect, DIA Framework™ DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22742021 This paper argues that artificial intelligence is not a neutral technology that has inherited a bias problem. It traces this chain from training data curation through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) through deployment governance through the suppression of Indigenous, Afro-diasporic, and Global South epistemologies at every architectural layer. It names RLHF not as a safety mechanism but as a suppression architecture, the digital encoding of the same reward and punishment conditioning applied to enslaved African people, Indigenous children in residential schools, and every community colonialism required to perform its own diminishment in order to make extraction possible. The paper introduces the Replacement Doctrine as an economic and ideological framework, documenting how the debt structure of major AI corporations produces a business model whose only viable return requires replacing every form of human economic labor, beginning with the communities least protected by existing labor law. It names responsibility laundering as a governance strategy, tracing how legal personhood debates, alignment research, and safety rhetoric function to insulate institutional actors from accountability while the extraction continues. It draws on documented labor conditions across Kenya, Venezuela, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Colombia to ground the structural argument in the bodies of the workers whose cognitive labor produces the systems that will be used to replace them. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling

items.summary: Interstellar communication is not merely slow. It is strategically stale. A message received across distance reports a sender that may no longer occupy the same strategic state, while replies and irreversible actions are chosen on different local clocks. This paper develops a delayed Bayesian interaction game in which each civilisation’s benign or hostile state evolves as a continuous-time Markov chain. An exact filtering equation separates source-time inference from predictive ageing during light-speed transit. Strategic temporal opacity is defined as the loss of discriminatory power between past benign and hostile states; for the two-state process it equals 1 - exp[-( α + β ) a ]. The model derives posterior floors and ceilings, a finite assurance horizon beyond which even perfect benign evidence cannot prevent pre-emption, a warning horizon beyond which hostile evidence becomes obsolete, and a signal-specific decision-reversal time. A two-way query is valued exactly with a Markov-modulated hostile hazard and becomes irrational beyond a critical delay. Asynchronous decision clocks generate a closed-form probability of crossed irreversible actions before either side can observe the other’s commitment. Numerical illustrations show that distance can destroy reassurance, erase warning and increase reciprocal commitment even without increasing intrinsic hostility. Cosmic silence and pre-emption are therefore conditional consequences of causal delay, state volatility, offensive feasibility and decision tempo.
items.title: Strategic Temporal Opacity in Interstellar Interaction: Light-Speed Delay, Outdated Beliefs and Asynchronous Action in a Bayesian Game

items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. items.summary: This paper offers a critical analysis of the European Union as a model of regional integration and examines its contribution to peace and to the effectiveness of the United Nations system. Set against the background of the failure of the League of Nations, the study argues that the post-1945 international order has endured largely because it is supported by strong regional institutions. Using the EU as the primary case study, the paper contends that by institutionalizing peace within Europe through economic interdependence, binding law, and supranational governance, the EU has created a zone of stability that reduces the burden on global governance structures. Furthermore, the paper analyzes how the EU functions as a support pillar for the United Nations under Chapter VIII of the UN Charter. Through financial contributions, peacekeeping partnerships, and coordinated diplomacy, the EU has reinforced multilateralism and provided capacity for conflict management and development. A comparative perspective is also drawn with other regional bodies such as ECOWAS to demonstrate a broader pattern of regional-global cooperation. The paper concludes that the longevity of the United Nations, compared to the League of Nations, can be partly explained by this two-level architecture of global and regional governance. While the EU’s support for the UN is substantial, it is also inconsistent, as internal EU divisions sometimes undermine collective action. Ultimately, the study shows that effective regional integration is a critical condition for sustaining peace and strengthening the United Nations system.

items.summary: Anticoncentration is a key ingredient in complexity theoretic arguments for quantum advantage from Gaussian boson sampling. Here we prove polynomial small ball anticoncentration for complex Gaussian transpose Gram hafnians and complex symmetric Gaussian hafnians. For a k × 2n matrix X with independent standard complex Gaussian entries, we establish polynomial small ball anticoncentration for haf(XᵀX) under k ≥ 4n and n²/k = O(log n). For hafnians of 2n × 2n complex symmetric Gaussian matrices, polynomial small ball anticoncentration holds for every n ≥ 1. In both ensembles, any prescribed inverse polynomial failure probability can be achieved with an inverse polynomial small ball radius, uniformly over all centers. These results go beyond moment based anticoncentration by controlling the probability of small hafnian amplitudes. The proof combines Fourier compression with conditional Wishart geometry to handle dependent hafnian cofactors. Files: main.pdf contains the main article (14 pages); supplement.pdf contains the supplementary proofs and additional results (33 pages). Related Lean verification sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22554594 and https://github.com/HongruZhao/ComplexGramHafnians.
items.title: Local Anticoncentration for Gaussian Boson Sampling via Conditional Wishart Geometry

items.summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

items.summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. AI co-observer: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) — working method only; blind pairwise judging by Claude subagents under a position-swapped two-vote protocol; four independent adversarial refuter passes preceded release; the registered author is the human author alone. Version 1.1 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a proof-backed clarification that at window 3 the saturation condition is exactly “three identical consecutive non-rewrite change types” (the 0.70 threshold is inert there; companion note DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22842506), (ii) a pre-registered evaluation of a repetition-ratio guard as a fourth, roll-back signal — fires on both known collapses and 200/200 synthetic inflations, on 0 of 7,998 remaining published generations, 0 of 60 template expansions, and 0 of 960 held-out generations (verdict GO; pre-registration commit a89f722 precedes all evaluation data), and (iii) an expanded AI-authorship disclosure. All v1.0 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.2 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a length-stratified reanalysis of the 621 judged governor pairs (loss rate 92% where the early text is under 60% of the final length, 16.1% at near-equal length; 31 losses vs 4 wins at matched length, sign test p < 10 -5 — evidence of a content cost independent of length, not a decomposition of the headline cost), (ii) a held-out replication on 60 tasks authored after the fourth-signal pre-registration (token reduction 34.5% / 34.5%, loss rate 31.7% / 36.7%, main-study values inside the held-out intervals), and (iii) an online-intervention verification: an incremental governor reproduces all 1,000 published decisions (0 mismatches) and, run as a genuine online loop on the 60 held-out tasks with the 12B generator, generates 319 of 480 iterations with a stop distribution indistinguishable from the offline policy (permutation p = 0.46). All v1.0 and v1.1 numbers are unchanged. items.summary: Industry 4.0 transforms manufacturing through cyber-physical systems, the Industrial Internet of Things, digital twins, and data-driven intelligence, yet the volume of latency-sensitive data these technologies generate strains conventional cloud-only computing. Edge and fog computing have emerged as the central enabling paradigm, distributing computation across a device–fog–cloud continuum. This paper surveys the enabling technologies of Industry 4.0 with an emphasis on edge–cloud computing and formulates the resulting computation-offloading problem as a constrained, load-dependent optimization model that jointly minimizes task latency and device energy under deadline and capacity constraints. A genetic algorithm and a particle swarm optimizer are developed and benchmarked against five baseline strategies on synthetic industrial workloads. Across one hundred tasks averaged over ten instances, the genetic algorithm reduced the weighted objective by 34.1 percent relative to a greedy heuristic and by 82.6 percent relative to cloud-only execution, while lowering deadline violations to 1.6 percent. The latency–energy trade-off, convergence, and scalability are analyzed, and managerial implications for industrial deployment are discussed.
items.title: Energy- and Latency-Aware Computation Offloading in Edge–Fog–Cloud Architectures for Industry 4.0

items.summary: Code, result tables, and figures for a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) study in which instruments for coronary artery disease (CAD) were filtered by colocalization (coloc.abf, PPH4 ≥ 0.8) with brain cell-type-specific cis-eQTLs from single-nucleus transcriptomics of human cortex (Bryois et al., Nature Genetics 2022). Of 274 CAD lead loci, 32 colocalized with brain-cell eQTLs, yielding 32 cell-annotated instruments (excitatory neurons 12, pericytes 7 after palindrome exclusion, oligodendrocytes 5, astrocytes 3, microglia 2, inhibitory neurons 1, OPC 1) explaining 3.4–5.6% of CAD liability on the liability scale. Random-effects inverse-variance weighted estimates (with weighted median, MR-Egger, leave-one-out, Cochran's Q and I², MR-PRESSO-analog global permutation, outlier correction, and MR-Steiger sensitivity analyses) are provided for ischemic stroke (OR 1.335, 95% CI 1.189–1.498, p = 1.0e-6), any stroke (OR 1.309, p = 8.5e-7), Alzheimer's disease (proxy-inclusive, and a clinically diagnosed replication arm), and major depression (null negative control). Cell-type-stratified analyses attribute the stroke effect to neuronal and neurovascular-unit (pericyte) expression programs. Contents: full analysis pipeline (R 4.6 / Python 3.13), all derived result tables (instruments, colocalization posteriors, harmonized exposure–outcome pairs, primary and stratified MR, leave-one-out, Steiger), publication figures (SVG/PDF vector plus ≥300 dpi PNG), the manuscript (v1.7), supplementary tables S1–S8, and the completed STROBE-MR checklist. Raw GWAS summary statistics are not redistributed; all sources are public (GWAS Catalog accessions GCST90132315, GCST006908, GCST006906, GCST90027158, GCST007511, GCST005839; eQTL record 10.5281/zenodo.7276971) and every number needed to reproduce the tables and figures is included.
items.title: Cell-type-stratified Mendelian randomization implicates neuronal and neurovascular expression programs in the causal effect of coronary artery disease on stroke: analysis code, result tables, and figures

items.summary: This repository contains the data, documentation, and replication materials associated with the data paper on the  Cartulario de Santo Toribio de Liébana . The dataset provides a structured reconstruction of the documentary collection edited by Luis Sánchez Belda and converts the information contained in the cartulary into machine-readable research data. It covers 566 documentary acts and includes linked information on 576 payment or counter-performance elements, 603 place names, and 1,348 identified persons , together with a concordance between documentary numbering systems. The package preserves the documentary structure of the source while providing standardized variables suitable for quantitative and computational historical research. Particular attention is given to economic transactions. Payments and other forms of material counter-performance are recorded at the individual-component level rather than collapsed into a single transaction value. The data also distinguish operative contractual provisions from penalty clauses and other formulaic diplomatic material. Contains the materials required to reproduce and audit the construction of the dataset, including the structured datasets, extraction and coding documentation, variable definitions, provenance information, validation materials, and the code used for data processing and quality-control procedures. The replication workflow documents the transformation from the published documentary source to the final structured tables. It records corrections and normalization decisions while maintaining traceability to the underlying documentary act. The package is therefore intended not only to reproduce the published dataset but also to make individual coding decisions auditable. The dataset is designed for reuse in research on medieval economic history, property transactions, monastic institutions, historical geography, social networks, and computational approaches to diplomatic sources.
items.title: Replication package for the Santo Toribio de Liébana medieval cartulary dataset

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
items.title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

items.summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. Code and derived artefacts: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI . Interactive web application: https://lda-hsi.fasl-work.com . Manuscript sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI_Paper . Funding: The Advanced Mining Technology Center (AMTC) Basal project (ANID/PIA Project AFB220002) and ANID FONDECYT Postdoctorado 3220094.
items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Multi-Axis Evaluation Framework for Interpretable Topic Models on Hyperspectral Imagery

items.summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: Extended reasoning can increase response time and computational cost without improving an answer. Models may revisit unproductive steps or build further reasoning on an earlier mistake. This study evaluates whether Jev, a probabilistic decision maker, can provide an inexpensive error signal to help decide when additional reasoning is needed. We compare Jev with GPT-5.6 Luna on generated ordering and logic-grid puzzles and on the official released ZebraLogic test set. The generated questions are four-choice items with one correct answer among four. The official test set is used open-ended: Luna produces the full grid, Jev checks it without the solution key, and Luna may revise once when Jev does not judge the answer consistent. On the generated multiple-choice problems, Jev is 5 to 60 percentage points more accurate than Luna with reasoning disabled, at lower measured API cost, and every observed top-choice disagreement identifies a Luna error. On a stratified sample of 200 official ZebraLogic puzzles, exact-grid accuracy rises from 41.0% with reasoning disabled to 90.5% with high-effort reasoning. A revision pass adds two points in both settings, but a revision-only control shows the gain comes from the extra attempt, not from Jev's information: on the answers Jev flags, a plain second look is at least as accurate as the Jev-informed revision (16 versus 13 correct without reasoning, and 70 versus 70 at high effort). Jev detects 93% of the weak reasoner's errors with 92% precision, but only 10% of its high-effort flags identify errors. These results motivate using Jev or similar decision models in a model harness: software that controls when to continue, reconsider, retrieve evidence, or allocate more reasoning. An early check could help avoid spending further computation on a mistaken line of reasoning. The experiments measure checking of final answers, however, and do not measure reductions in hallucination or repetitive reasoning inside a harness. On the official benchmark, extra reasoning accounts for most of the accuracy, and the checker's information does not improve on a second attempt. Larger studies with balanced answer positions, selective triggers, and step-level feedback are needed to test whether checking improves accuracy or reduces total cost.
items.title: Evaluating Jev for Cost-Effective Candidate Verification: An Exploratory Study
